https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Peter Hall said there will be ‘more violence and more death’ if domestic abusers are included in the early prison release scheme. Photograph: Karen Robinson/The Observer View image in fullscreen Peter Hall said there will be ‘more violence and more death’ if domestic abusers are included in the early prison release scheme. Photograph: Karen Robinson/The Observer Domestic violence More women will die if domestic abusers leave prison early, victim’s parents warn Parents of Michaela Hall, whose partner killed her after he left prison in 2021, say Probation Service cannot cope with mass release Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent Mon 17 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More women will die if ministers include domestic abusers in the early prison release scheme, the parents of a woman murdered by her partner shortly after he was freed have warned. Michaela Hall, a 49-year-old charity worker, was killed in her home in Cornwall, by Lee Kendall in 2021 two weeks after he was released from prison, where he had been serving a sentence for assaulting her. The Probation Service incorrectly assessed Kendall as medium risk, despite the fact he had strangled Hall, threatened her with weapons and police had received 34 pieces ofintelligence about his abuse against her. At an inquest into her death , probation staff cited “horrendous work pressures” as part of the reason why the error was made. Hall’s parents, Anne and Peter, said domestic abuse victims across the country would be “absolutely petrified” at the prospect of their abusers being released early. “There’s going to be more violence and there’s going to be more death. It’s very simple,” Peter said. “The Probation Service can’t cope on a day-to-day basis. They certainly can’t cope with 5,000 prisoners being released. It’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever heard.” From October, the government is planning to release 5,000 offenders in England and Wales earlier than scheduled to create more space in overcrowded prisons. Probation officers have voted overwhelmingly in favour of potential strike action over excessive workloads and the chief inspector of probation for England and Wales , Martin Jones, has said he does not think the system will be able to cope. Prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming charges will be excluded from early release after an intervention by the prime minister , Andy Burnham, in response to backlash over the plans. Farah Nazeer, the chief executive of Women’s Aid, said it was “really upsetting and troubling” that domestic abuse perpetrators would not be excluded. “We’re releasing prisoners early when they won’t have had proper rehabilitation. Probation is probably not able to manage them effectively. They’re going to be angry. Where do you think they’re going to go first? It’s absolutely appalling,” she said. “Women will die as a result of this. There is no doubt in my mind. Survivors need to come forward and they need to seek help.” Nazeer criticised the government for failing to give survivors enough time to prepare for the early release and said it would “completely undermine” Labour’s goal to halve violence against women in a decade. “You can’t have a halving violence against women strategy and then choose to release the perpetrators of the biggest crime against women and children early,” she said. “Why does the government think it’s OK to trade women’s safety up?” The government has announced £10m for victim support, a national helpline and greater involvement for victims in setting licence conditions, but Nazeer said this was not enough to help inundated support services. “We’re having to refuse 50% of women and children into refuge because the funding isn’t there,” she said. “£10m doesn’t even begin to cut it against the need that’s out there.” The Hall family have launched a legal challenge under the Human Rights Act against the Probation Service and police over their handling of Hall’s case. While the service miscategorised Kendall’s risk level, meaning he was released with minimal supervision, police officers also failed to enter Hall’s property on the night she was murdered despite a call from a friend saying she was being attacked. As they drove away, one officer said: “What can you do if she don’t help herself?” Anne said: “Our daughter was stabbed by some evil person that should never have been anywhere near her because they all didn’t do their jobs properly. “It’s left two children without their mum and the rest of the family absolutely shattered. It was a catalogue of mistakes, laziness and victim blaming which is the most dreadful thing that you can do.” Peter said the aim of the legal action was to get justice for his daughter but also to help prevent future deaths. “This won’t help us, it doesn’t make us feel any better,” he said. “We are only doing this to bring about change and so other people don’t have to suffer. We hear so much nowadays that these services are just not doing their job properly.” Catherine Knight, the deputy head of legal at the Good Law Project, which is acting for the family, said: “We would hope [the legal challenge] would force the authorities to change the way they operate. “If the government wants to go ahead with the early release scheme then we need to ensure the systems supporting offenders and victims are robust and do work as they should but, at present, there are systemic issues within the service.” A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The murder of Michaela Hall was a horrific crime, and our thoughts remain with her loved ones. “We have always stated we wanted to go further to protect the public, and we are fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most dangerous offenders behind bars. That’s on top of murderers, anyone on life sentences and those in prison for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences who are already blocked from any changes. “Our record £700m investment in probation is ensuring staff have the resources, powers and technology they need to manage offenders safely in the community, and we are tagging a record number of offenders to track their every move, alongside investing a record £550m in victim support.” Explore more on these topics Domestic violence Violence against women and girls Femicide Prisons and probation UK criminal justice England Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.dw.com/en/kazakhstan-s-futur.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JAKj People in Astana and all other cities in Kazakhstan are headed to the polls on Sunday Image: Roman Sigaev/Zoonar/picture alliance Advertisement On August 23, Kazakhstan , a former Soviet country that has recently adopted a new constitution, will hold elections to its parliament. The legislative body will be transformed from a two-chamber to a single-chamber system. Citizens will elect 145 members of parliament via party lists. All seven registered parties have been admitted to the election, including the ruling party, Adilet (which translates to "Justice"). But the election result is the least of the campaign's intrigues. Experts DW interviewed agree that no party other than President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's Adilet stands a chance of winning. Consolidation of power in the president's hands Luca Anceschi, Professor of Eurasian Studies at the University of Glasgow, Scotland, suggests that the new parliament will do the same as the previous one, "which is pretty much to represent whatever the regime wants them to do." In his view, one should not expect representatives of the genuine opposition to be elected to parliament. Stefan Meister, Head of the Center for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), shares this assessment. He says the ruling party is likely to win the election, a scenario also reflected in recent opinion polls. Both experts agree that these elections are intended to consolidate Tokayev's power and further weaken the bloc led by Nursultan Nazarbayev , the country's president from 1991-2019. Constitutional amendments approved earlier allow Tokayev to seek another seven-year presidential term in 2029 and replace the two-chamber parliament with a single-chamber assembly called the Kurultai. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev voted in the referendum on a new constitution for his country on March 15, 2026 Image: Kazakh Presidential Press Service/REUTERS According to former Kazakhstani senator Zauresh Battalova, who now heads the NGO Foundation for the Development of Parliamentarism in Kazakhstan, what matters is not the number of chambers in parliament, but "the scope of its powers, its autonomy and its ability to oversee the executive branch of government." The new constitution has changed not only the structure of parliament but also the way its members are elected. Independent candidates are no longer allowed to run under the current electoral system. Zauresh Battalova sees this as one of the factors limiting voters' political choice. "The election will be held exclusively on the basis of party lists, in the absence of a political opposition and with limited party competition. The scope for genuine political choice remains extremely narrow," she told DW. Kazakhstan's democratic backlash: Will Europe react? Meister and Anceschi both say that one should not expect any reaction from European Union members or the European Commission to the deterioration in political freedoms in Kazakhstan. Meister points out that, since the start of the war in Ukraine , the EU has adopted a more pragmatic approach towards Central Asian states. Europe is now interested in developing trade routes as an alternative to those via Russia, as well as in the region's abundant resources. In his view, the only bodies likely to react to the current situation in Kazakhstan are civil society organizations, the European Parliament or the Council of Europe. The election campaign ahead of Kazakhstan's parliamentary elections involves more than just posters and info flyers Image: Anatolij Weißkopf/DW "The days when the European Union and individual EU member states were more critical of the rule of law and governance in Central Asia are gone, unfortunately," Anceschi says. The University of Glasgow professor notes that an authoritarian backslide is taking place not only in Kazakhstan but also in other EU partner countries. As for Kazakhstan itself, says Meister, it remains the least repressive authoritarian country in the region, with at least some space for civil society, albeit one that is narrowing. "Wherever you buy your oil and gas from, you are never going to buy it from a democracy ― unless it is Norway. So, in that sense, there is not much of a choice," Anceschi says. In 2025, Kazakhstan became the second-largest oil exporter to the EU, with a total share of 12.8%, amounting to 55.8 million tons of crude oil, surpassed only by the United States, according to the European Council of the EU . The future of Kazakhstan's foreign policy Experts acknowledge that Kazakhstan has managed to remain neutral in the standoff between Russia and Europe against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine. Maintaining this course may prove difficult. "They are affected by the conflict, but they are not participating," says Anceschi, describing the country's current position as a "geopolitical comfort zone." How can Kazakhstan navigate ties with Russia and China? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Kazakhstan has not officially opposed the European sanctions against Russia , nor has it joined them. "Of course, it is a task with only one ultimate goal, which is the preservation of authoritarian rule," Anceschi says. "So even in this case, foreign policy is becoming an instrument for achieving internal stability." Meister, in turn, draws attention to the increasing level of cooperation between the Central Asian states, which, facing significant external pressure, tend to act as a single bloc while actively seeking to reduce tensions among themselves. He suggests that Kazakhstan is interested in diversifying its external relations not only with the EU, Russia and China, but also with other world powers, such as Arab or East Asian states. According to Meister, Kazakhstan "does not want to be too dependent on Russia ― it has seen what Russia is doing in Ukraine ― and it does not want to be dependent on China." So, the country is looking for alternatives, and Europe could be one of them, both as a market for its resources and as a potential investor in Kazakhstan's economy. https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4597.text: Slovakia and Poland have signed a letter of intent to deepen bilateral cooperation in defence and the defence industry under the EU’s SAFE instrument. The agreement was signed on Monday in Nowa Dęba by Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák (SMER-SD) and his Polish counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The cooperation will focus on two areas — ammunition production and Poland’s SAN programme for countering drones. Kaliňák said Slovakia wants to contribute to the security of its neighbours and praised Poland as a leader in military modernisation in Europe. He also highlighted Poland’s counter-drone capabilities. Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, praised Slovakia’s experience and production capacity, particularly in ammunition manufacturing. He also thanked Slovakia for providing recently purchased radars to help protect Polish airspace as part of NATO’s Eastern Sentry operation. The Slovak Minister was in Nowa Dęba as an honorary guest at a demonstration involving the 18th Mechanised Division’s combat group. Source: TASR

Among those invited are Chancellor Friedrich Merz , Bundestag President Julia Klöckner and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier . In a speech released to the press in advance, Steinmeier stressed the importance of the court at a time when the liberal democracy in Germany was increasing threatened by "forces at the political margins." "A strong Constitutional Court is part of the resilience of our democracy," he said. "I am convinced that the Constitutional Court is a guarantee that, despite all challenges, the success story of our liberal democracy will continue." Steinmeier highlighted the importance of the Constitutional Court in moving Germany "away from the traditional authoritarian state toward a modern civil society" after the Nazi era . "The court succeeded in positioning itself ... against the Nazi tyranny and to use its jurisdiction to stress that the constitution was and is a deliberate counter-model to this tyranny," he said. The Constitutional Court, which was founded on September 28, 1951, is the highest German court for constitutional issues and is tasked with ensuring the compliance of all governmental institutions with the German constitution, or Basic Law . Up to the end of 2025, it dealt with almost 274,000 cases, more than 96% of which were judicial reviews following constitutional complaints, according to the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb). The 51-year-old Wüst is the first premier of the state to make an official visit to Turkey. https://p.dw.com/p/5NNvY Skip next section Rhine levels in Cologne hit record low after dry September 09/28/2026 September 28, 2026 Rhine levels in Cologne hit record low after dry September Mark Hallam Freight ships along the Rhine are being forced to run with vastly reduced loads to avoid grounding out, with water levels still well below usual after the hot and dry summer [FILE: September 23, 2026] Image: Thomas Frey/dpa/picture alliance Even as October approaches, the water levels on the crucial River Rhine remain among the lowest on record. After an unusually dry September, the reading in Cologne dipped to 40 centimeters (just under 16 inches) on Monday morning, monitoring data from the WSV agency showed . "The 40 centimeters consitutes a low-water record," a Cologne city official, Markus Neumann, told the DPA news agency. Prior to the series of new records in the past few months, the lowest measurement in Cologne had been a 2018 reading of 69 centimeters. Several of the points along western Europe's busiest inland freight waterway were similarly shallow on Monday. In Koblenz, Andernach, and Düsseldorf the readings even moved into negative territory, meaning that the gauging station was completely dry. The levels at the measuring points do not indicate the absolute depth of the river for shipping, but rather the depth at a more accessible point nearer the banks. The difference between the depth and the readings varies among the gauging stations but tends to be somwhere around 1 meter shallower than the navigable shipping channel. Amid a hot and dry summer, the Rhine made headlines repeatedly and hit a series of record lows in August , severely impacting commercial shipping. A brief rainy period had brought some relief but levels had been dropping again in the last few weeks. The Rhine, linking the Netherlands and the vast port of Rotterdam to much of western Germany, is used for an array of freight transportation, including coal and fuel. Germany's WSV river agency also had low water level warnings in place on stretches of most of the country's major rivers on Monday, including the Elbe, Danube, Weser, Ems and the Oder.
